mis.m: Counts every dot one by one on a ten frame or dot card instead of seeing the amount at a glance.
mis.why: The student has not yet linked the arrangement to a known quantity, so counting by ones feels safest.
mis.fix: Flash a ten frame for two seconds, hide it, and ask 'How many? How did you see it?' Start with 5 and 10 so the full row and full frame become anchors.

mis.m: Says 7 for a ten frame showing 8 because they see 'the top row and some more' without noticing how many empty boxes there are.
mis.why: The student looks at the filled boxes only and guesses the extra part.
mis.fix: Ask 'How many are missing to make 10?' so students use the empty boxes: 2 empty means 8.

mis.m: Recognizes the dice pattern for 6 but cannot name 6 when the dots are shown in a ten frame or as fingers.
mis.why: The student memorized one picture rather than the quantity, so a new arrangement feels like a new number.
mis.fix: Show the same number in three arrangements side by side (dice, ten frame, fingers) and ask 'What is the same? What is different?'

cra.c: Students build quick images with counters on ten frames, dot cards, rekenreks and fingers, then flash them to a partner who names the amount without counting.
cra.r: Students match dot cards, ten frame cards and finger pictures that show the same amount, and sketch a ten frame to show how they saw it, such as '5 and 3 more.'
cra.a: Students write the number and a short number sentence for how they saw it, such as 5 + 3 = 8 or 10 - 2 = 8.
cra.look: Students call out amounts quickly after a brief flash and explain what they saw, like 'a full row and 2 more.'

assess: How did you know it was 8 so fast?
Did you look at the dots or the empty boxes?
advance: Can you see 8 a different way? Show your partner.
If I add one more dot, what will it be without counting?

assess: What part did you see first?
How many empty boxes are there?
advance: How does a full top row help you?
Can you find two cards that show the same number?

assess: Point to the full row. How many is that?
Show me 5 on your fingers.
advance: Is this more than 5 or less than 5?
How many more to fill the row?
support: Use only 5-frames and amounts up to 5 at first, then add a second row.
Let the student build the arrangement with counters before the quick flash.

stems: There are ___ empty boxes, so it is ___.
I saw it a different way. I saw ___.
This card and that card both show ___.
d: Recognize instantly the quantity of structured arrangements.

mis.m: Thinks 34 can only be made as 3 tens and 4 ones, so says 2 tens and 14 ones is a different number.
mis.why: The student has seen only the standard way and does not yet see that 1 ten can become 10 ones.
mis.fix: Have the student unbundle one ten-stick of cubes into 10 loose cubes and count all again to see the total did not change.

mis.m: For a number like 112, writes 1 hundred, 1 ten, 2 ones as 1,000 + 10 + 2 or reads the blocks as 'one hundred twelve' while building 1 hundred and 12 tens.
mis.why: Numbers past 100 are new, and students mix up how many tens belong in the number.
mis.fix: Build 100 as 10 tens, then add tens and ones one at a time while counting aloud: 100, 110, 111, 112.

mis.m: Counts each ten rod as 1 when finding the total, so 4 tens and 3 ones becomes 7.
mis.why: The student counts the objects, not what each object is worth.
mis.fix: Have students count by tens while touching each rod: '10, 20, 30, 40,' then switch to ones: '41, 42, 43.'

cra.c: Students bundle straws or snap cubes into tens and use base-ten blocks to build a number such as 46 in two or three ways, trading a ten for 10 ones each time.
cra.r: Students draw quick pictures with sticks for tens and dots for ones and record each way on a place value chart with hundreds, tens and ones.
cra.a: Students write each way as a sentence or equation, such as 46 = 4 tens 6 ones = 3 tens 16 ones = 40 + 6.
cra.look: Students trade a ten for ten ones, count the total again, and show partners that both ways make the same number.

assess: How do you know 3 tens and 16 ones is still 46?
What did you do to the ten you broke apart?
advance: How many different ways can you make 46? How do you know you found them all?
Show 110 using no hundreds.

assess: How many tens did you draw? How many ones?
What does each stick in your picture stand for?
advance: Can you trade one more ten? What happens?
How would you make 105 with a hundred?

assess: How many cubes are in this stick?
Count these tens with me.
advance: If I break this ten apart, how many cubes do we get?
Is it still the same number?
support: Use pre-made ten-sticks and loose cubes on a two-column tens and ones mat.
Start with numbers under 30 so there are only a few trades.

stems: I made ___ with ___ tens and ___ ones.
Another way is ___ tens and ___ ones.
d: Use concrete and pictorial models to compose and decompose numbers up to 120 in more than one way as so many hundreds, so many tens, and so many ones.

mis.m: Writes 'sixty-four' as 604 or 60 4.
mis.why: The student writes the number the way it sounds instead of using place value.
mis.fix: Use place value cards: lay the 4 card on top of the zero in the 60 card so students see 64 is 60 + 4 written together.

mis.m: Writes 47 in expanded form as 4 + 7.
mis.why: The student sees the digits but not the value of the 4 in the tens place.
mis.fix: Build 47 with base-ten blocks and ask 'How much are the tens worth?' before writing 40 + 7.

mis.m: Mixes up teen numbers, such as writing 61 for 'sixteen' or reading 17 as 'seventy-one.'
mis.why: The teen number names say the ones first, which is the opposite of how the digits are written.
mis.fix: Show teen numbers on a ten frame pair: 1 full ten and 6 more. Say '1 ten and 6 ones is 16' while pointing to each digit.

cra.c: Students build numbers up to 120 with base-ten blocks, bundled straws or ten frames and say the number aloud.
cra.r: Students draw quick pictures of tens and ones, match them to number cards and fill in a place value chart.
cra.a: Students write the same number in standard form and expanded form, such as 85 and 80 + 5, and match it to its number word.
cra.look: Students move between blocks, quick pictures, standard form and expanded form for the same number and check that they match.

assess: How does your picture match 80 + 5?
Why is the 8 worth 80?
advance: How would you write 108 in expanded form? What happens to the tens?
Can you build a number that has 0 ones?

assess: How many tens are in your picture? How did you write them?
Which part of 63 shows the tens?
advance: Can you write it a different way?
What number is 1 hundred, 1 ten and 5 ones?

assess: Show me the tens. Show me the ones.
Which card says 40?
advance: Put the 7 card on top of the 40 card. What number is it now?
Is 47 more or less than 74?
support: Give place value cards (tens cards and ones cards) to build the number.
Use a tens and ones mat with a picture of a stick and a dot at the top.

d: Use objects, pictures, and expanded and standard forms to represent numbers up to 120.

mis.m: When asked for a number greater than 58, gives 50 or 49 because it has a 5 or looks 'bigger' in some way.
mis.why: The student focuses on one digit and does not yet compare the whole number.
mis.fix: Have the student find 58 on a hundred chart and point to numbers that come after it, then say 'After means greater.'

mis.m: Only gives the very next number, such as 59 for 'greater than 58,' and thinks no other answer works.
mis.why: The student thinks there is one right answer.
mis.fix: Ask for three different greater numbers and list them on the board, then ask 'Are they all greater? How do you know?'

mis.m: For 'less than 101' says 110 because both numbers start with 1 and have a 1 and a 0.
mis.why: Numbers past 100 have the same digits in new orders, which is confusing to read.
mis.fix: Build both numbers with base-ten blocks and compare the tens: 101 has 0 tens and 110 has 1 ten.

cra.c: Students build a given number with base-ten blocks or cubes, then add or take away a ten or some ones to make a number that is greater or less.
cra.r: Students use a hundred chart (to 120) or a number line and mark a number to the right for greater or to the left for less.
cra.a: Students write the new number and say the comparison, such as '72 is greater than 68.'
cra.look: Students point to a hundred chart or number line to show where a greater or less number is and give more than one answer.

assess: How do you know 72 is greater than 68?
What did you change to make it greater?
advance: Give a number that is greater than 68 but less than 70.
What number is 10 less? How did you find it?

assess: Where is your number on the chart? Is it before or after?
Did you add tens or ones?
advance: Can you find a greater number that has the same ones digit?
Give me a number less than 100 but more than 95.

assess: Show me the number. Point to one that comes after.
Is this number bigger or smaller?
advance: Add one more cube. Is it greater now?
What comes just before this number?
support: Use a number path with numbers to 30 before the full hundred chart.
Give two choices and ask which is greater.

stems: I added ___ to make it greater.
I took away ___ to make it less.
d: Generate a number that is greater than or less than a given whole number up to 120.

mis.m: Says 39 is greater than 41 because 9 is greater than 1.
mis.why: The student compares the ones digits first instead of the tens.
mis.fix: Build both numbers with base-ten blocks and ask 'Who has more tens?' before looking at the ones.

mis.m: Says 100 is less than 99 because 100 has zeros and zero means nothing.
mis.why: The student sees zero as 'nothing' and does not know its place value role.
mis.fix: Build 99 with blocks, add one more cube, trade for a ten and then trade 10 tens for a hundred so students see 100 grow from 99.

mis.m: Uses 'bigger' and 'smaller' loosely and cannot explain which number is 'greater than' or 'less than' in a full sentence.
mis.why: The comparative language is new and students have used everyday words.
mis.fix: Post a sentence frame with pictures ('___ is greater than ___') and have partners say it every time they compare.

cra.c: Partners build two numbers with base-ten blocks and line up the tens and ones side by side to see which has more.
cra.r: Students draw quick pictures of each number or find both on a hundred chart, then circle the tens to compare.
cra.a: Students say and write the comparison in words: '73 is greater than 37 because 7 tens is more than 3 tens.'
cra.look: Students compare tens first, then ones, and use the words greater than, less than and equal to in full sentences.

assess: Why did you look at the tens first?
How do you know 56 is greater than 52?
advance: What number could go here to make it less than 64?
How would you compare 110 and 101?

assess: How many tens does each number have?
Show me where both numbers are on the chart.
advance: If the tens are the same, what do you look at next?
Can you find a number that is equal to 4 tens and 5 ones?

assess: Which pile has more tens?
Point to the greater number.
advance: Say it with me: '__ is greater than __.'
Which one is less?
support: Use blocks for both numbers every time and line them up.
Give a sentence frame card with a picture for greater and less.

stems: I looked at the tens first. ___ has more tens.
The tens are the same, so I looked at the ones.
d: Use place value to compare whole numbers up to 120 using comparative language.

mis.m: Orders 105, 98, 110 as 98, 110, 105 because 'one-ten' sounds like it should come before 'one hundred five.'
mis.why: Numbers past 100 are new and students rely on how they sound.
mis.fix: Build each number with blocks, then place them on a number line counting by tens from 90 to 120.

mis.m: Places numbers on an open number line with no thought to spacing, such as putting 50 very close to 10 and far from 90.
mis.why: The student sees the line as a row of boxes, not a distance.
mis.fix: Mark 0, 50 and 100 first as landmarks and ask 'Is 23 closer to 0 or 50?' before placing it.

mis.m: Orders numbers from greatest to least when asked for least to greatest, or reverses the direction partway through.
mis.why: The student does not yet hold the meaning of 'least' and 'greatest' while working.
mis.fix: Label the left end 'least' and the right end 'greatest' on the number line and have students check each number by asking 'Is it more than the one before?'

cra.c: Students hold number cards and line themselves up in order on a floor number line or clothesline, using base-ten blocks to check.
cra.r: Students place numbers on an open number line with landmarks such as 0, 50, 100 and 120, or on a hundred chart, and say why each spot makes sense.
cra.a: Students write the numbers in order from least to greatest or greatest to least and explain using tens and ones.
cra.look: Students move number cards on a clothesline or open number line and explain placements with tens and ones.

assess: Why did you put 67 before 76?
How did you decide where 85 goes on your line?
advance: Where would 115 go? Show me.
Which number is closest to 100? How do you know?

assess: Which landmark is this number close to?
How many tens does each number have?
advance: Can you add a number that goes between these two?
Put them in order from greatest to least now.

assess: Which number is the least? Point to it.
Does 40 come before or after 30?
advance: Count by tens with me. Where does 50 go?
Is this number more than the one before it?
support: Give a number line with tens already marked.
Order only three numbers with blocks before using the line.

stems: From least to greatest, the order is ___.
I put ___ near ___ on the number line.
d: Order whole numbers up to 120 using place value and open number lines.

mis.m: Writes 45 < 32 because the symbol 'looks right' or always puts the symbol pointing to the right.
mis.why: The student does not link the symbol's direction to which number is greater.
mis.fix: Have students write the words first ('45 is greater than 32'), then swap the words for the symbol and read it aloud left to right.

mis.m: Reads 28 > 82 as true because 8 is greater than 2.
mis.why: The student compares the ones digits instead of the tens.
mis.fix: Build both numbers with blocks and compare tens first: 2 tens and 8 tens.

mis.m: Uses = between numbers with the same digits, such as 34 = 43.
mis.why: The student sees the same digits and thinks the numbers match.
mis.fix: Build both numbers side by side and ask 'Do they have the same tens? The same ones?'

cra.c: Students build two numbers with base-ten blocks and place a symbol card (>, < or =) between them, then read the sentence aloud.
cra.r: Students draw quick pictures of each number or find both on a hundred chart and write the symbol between the pictures.
cra.a: Students write comparisons such as 67 > 59 and 40 = 40 and read each one aloud in words.
cra.look: Students read each comparison aloud from left to right with 'greater than,' 'less than' or 'equal to' and check it with blocks.

assess: Read your number sentence aloud. Does it make sense?
Why did you choose that symbol?
advance: What numbers could make ___ < 50 true?
Write the same comparison a different way.

assess: How do your blocks show which number is greater?
Which number has more tens?
advance: If I switch the two numbers, which symbol do you need?
Can you write a true sentence with =?

assess: Which number is greater? Point to it.
Read this with me: 30 is less than 50.
advance: Is 30 greater than 50 or less than 50?
Show me the symbol for 'less than.'
support: Give symbol cards with the words written under them.
Compare numbers to 20 with cubes before moving to 100.

stems: ___ is greater than ___, so I wrote >.
___ is less than ___, so I wrote <.
___ is equal to ___, so I wrote =.
I know because ___ has more tens.
d: Represent the comparison of two numbers to 100 using the symbols >, <, or =.

mis.why: The student adds the digits and ignores that 40 means 4 tens.
mis.fix: Build 40 with four ten-sticks and 7 loose cubes, then count by tens and ones together: 10, 20, 30, 40, 41 ... 47.

mis.m: Counts on by ones from 40 to add 7 tens, getting 47 for 40 + 70.
mis.why: The student does not notice the difference between a ten and a one.
mis.fix: Have students name each block before adding: 'Is this a ten or a one?'

mis.m: Writes the sum as 407 when adding 40 + 7.
mis.why: The student writes the numbers side by side, the way they hear them.
mis.fix: Use place value cards: put the 7 card on top of the 0 in the 40 card to make 47.

cra.c: Students use base-ten blocks, ten frames or bundled straws to show a multiple of ten and some ones, then put them together and count.
cra.r: Students draw quick pictures of tens and ones or jump on a number line from 40 by 7 ones.
cra.a: Students write equations such as 60 + 3 = 63 and 3 + 60 = 63 and explain using tens and ones.
cra.look: Students count by tens and then by ones to find sums and write the matching equation.

assess: Why is 60 + 3 equal to 63 and not 9?
How can you see the answer right away?
advance: What is 3 + 60? How do you know without counting?
Write a story for 50 + 8.

assess: How many tens did you draw?
Where did you start on the number line?
advance: What would 70 + 3 be? What changed?
Can you write it with the ones first?

assess: Count the tens with me.
Now count on the ones.
advance: How many ones are here?
What number do we have now?
support: Use ten frames and loose counters so tens and ones look different.
Start with 10 + a one-digit number, then 20 + a one-digit number.

stems: I counted by tens, then by ones.
d: Use concrete and pictorial models to determine the sum of a multiple of 10 and a one-digit number in problems up to 99.

mis.m: Adds every pair of numbers in a word problem, such as 'Ana has 5 stickers. Now she has 9. How many did she get?' becomes 5 + 9 = 14.
mis.why: The student looks for numbers and the word 'how many' and adds by habit.
mis.fix: Act it out with counters: start with 5, then ask 'How many do we need to add to get 9?'

mis.m: Solves 3 + [ ] = 7 by writing 10 in the box.
mis.why: The student reads the equation as 'add the numbers' and puts the answer in the box.
mis.fix: Have students build 3 cubes, then add cubes one at a time until there are 7, counting how many were added.

mis.m: In a comparing problem, such as 'Ben has 8 cars. Mia has 5. How many more does Ben have?' answers 8 or 13.
mis.why: Comparing needs matching two sets, which is harder than joining or separating.
mis.fix: Line up two rows of cubes one to one and ask 'How many in Ben's row have no partner?'

cra.c: Students act out joining, separating and comparing stories with counters, cubes or real objects on a work mat.
cra.r: Students draw pictures, part-part-whole mats or two rows of circles to show the story and mark the unknown with a box.
cra.a: Students write number sentences with the unknown in any position, such as 4 + [ ] = 9 or 12 - [ ] = 5, and tell how the sentence matches the story.
cra.look: Students act out or draw each story before writing an equation, and they place the unknown box where the story's missing part is.

assess: How did you know the missing part was at the start?
How does your picture match the story?
advance: Can you change the story so we need to subtract?
Write another number sentence that matches this story.

assess: Where is the missing part in your picture?
What does the box stand for?
advance: How else could you show this story?
Is this a joining, separating or comparing story? How do you know?

assess: How many did she start with? Show me.
Did she get more or give some away?
advance: Act it out with the cubes. What happens next?
How many are left now?
support: Read the story one sentence at a time and act out each part.
Use numbers within 10 first, then within 20.

d: Use objects and pictorial models to solve word problems involving joining, separating, and comparing sets within 20 and unknowns as any one of the terms in the problem such as 2 + 4 = [ ]; 3 + [ ] = 7; and 5 = [ ] - 3.

mis.m: Thinks there is only one way to make 10, such as 5 + 5.
mis.why: The student has practiced one pair and does not see that other pairs work.
mis.fix: Use a ten frame with two colors of counters and ask students to find a new way each time, then list all the ways.

mis.m: Adds three addends to make 10 but counts one counter twice, getting 11.
mis.why: The student loses track when there are more than two groups.
mis.fix: Have students move each counter into a ten frame as they count, so every box is filled once.

mis.m: Says 6 + 3 makes 10 because the ten frame 'looks almost full.'
mis.why: The student estimates instead of checking every box.
mis.fix: Ask 'Are there any empty boxes?' and have students count the empty boxes to see how many more are needed.

cra.c: Students fill ten frames with two or three colors of counters, use a rekenrek or shake and spill two-color counters to find ways to make 10.
cra.r: Students color ten frame pictures or draw ten in two or three groups, then record each way.
cra.a: Students write equations such as 6 + 4 = 10 and 2 + 3 + 5 = 10, and solve 10 = 7 + [ ] without objects.
cra.look: Students find many ways to make 10, check with a full ten frame and say equations aloud.

assess: How do you know you found all the ways with two numbers?
Can you make 10 with three numbers? Show me.
advance: If one part is 3, what must the other parts be?
What patterns do you see in your list?

assess: How many boxes are filled? How many are empty?
What does each color show?
advance: Can you change one color to make a new way?
Write your ten frame as a number sentence.

assess: Fill the ten frame. How many counters?
How many red? How many yellow?
advance: How many more to make 10?
Can you find another way?
support: Use a ten frame every time before writing equations.
Give a partly filled ten frame and ask only for the missing part.

stems: I know because the ten frame is full.
d: Compose 10 with two or more addends with and without concrete objects.

mis.m: For 8 + 5, counts all from 1 and gets lost, or counts on but includes the starting number, getting 12.
mis.why: The student does not yet trust a strategy and counting by ones causes errors.
mis.fix: Use two ten frames: fill the 8, move 2 from the 5 to make 10, and see 10 + 3 = 13.

mis.m: When making 10 for 9 + 6, breaks 6 into 1 and 5 but then adds 9 + 5 instead of 10 + 5.
mis.why: The student does the steps but forgets that the 1 went with the 9.
mis.fix: Have students move the counter physically and say '9 and 1 is 10, 10 and 5 is 15.'

mis.m: For 14 - 6, subtracts 4 and then subtracts 4 again instead of 2.
mis.why: The student does not track how much of the 6 is still left to take away.
mis.fix: Show 14 with ten frames, take 4 to get to 10, then ask 'How much of the 6 have we taken? How many more?'

cra.c: Students use double ten frames, counters and rekenreks to move counters and make a ten when adding or get back to ten when subtracting.
cra.r: Students draw ten frames or use a number line with a jump to 10 and then the rest.
cra.a: Students write the steps as number sentences, such as 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 10 + 3 = 13.
cra.look: Students move counters to fill a ten frame first and say how they broke apart a number to get to 10.

assess: Why did you break the 5 into 2 and 3?
How does making 10 help you?
advance: Would making 10 help with 7 + 6? Show me.
Can you solve 15 - 7 by getting to 10 first?

assess: Where did you jump to 10 on your number line?
How many did you move?
advance: Could you make 10 with the other number instead?
Which way is faster for you? Why?

assess: How many more does 8 need to make 10?
Show me the full ten frame.
advance: Now how many are left over?
What is 10 and 3?
support: Practice partners of 10 first so students know how many to move.
Use double ten frames with two colors for every problem.

stems: I took away ___ to get to 10.
d: Apply basic fact strategies to add and subtract within 20, including making 10 and decomposing a number leading to a 10.

mis.m: Gives only the answer, such as 'It's 12,' when asked to explain.
mis.why: The student thinks math talk means saying the answer.
mis.fix: Model a think-aloud with a full sentence, then ask 'What did you do first? What did you do next?'

mis.m: Says 'I counted' for every problem, even when a model shows a different strategy.
mis.why: The student does not yet have words for strategies like making 10 or using doubles.
mis.fix: Name strategies on an anchor chart with a picture for each, and point to the chart when a student uses one.

mis.m: Writes a number sentence that does not match what they did, such as 7 + 6 = 13 when they used 6 + 6 + 1.
mis.why: The student writes the problem, not the steps.
mis.fix: Ask the student to show each step with counters, then write one number sentence for each step.

cra.c: Students solve with counters, cubes or ten frames and then show a partner what they did with their hands.
cra.r: Students draw their work with ten frames, a number line or quick pictures and label the steps.
cra.a: Students write number sentences for each step and explain aloud, such as 'I used doubles: 6 + 6 = 12, so 6 + 7 = 13.'
cra.look: Students explain their strategies to partners using objects, drawings and number sentences, and listen to a different way.

assess: How is your strategy the same as your partner's? How is it different?
Why did you choose that strategy?
advance: Can you solve it another way and show both?
Which strategy would you use for 9 + 8? Why?

assess: Tell me what your picture shows.
Which number sentence matches this step?
advance: Can you write a number sentence for each step?
What strategy did you use? Find it on the chart.

assess: Show me with the counters what you did.
What did you do first?
advance: Then what did you do?
Can you say it in a sentence?
support: Give a strategy chart with pictures and one sentence frame.
Let students act out their strategy before talking.

stems: My way is the same as ___ because ___.
d: Explain strategies used to solve addition and subtraction problems up to 20 using spoken words, objects, pictorial models, and number sentences.

mis.m: Writes a story for 9 - 4 that is about adding, such as 'I had 9 apples and got 4 more.'
mis.why: The student focuses on the numbers and does not match the action to the symbol.
mis.fix: Act out the student's story with counters and ask 'Does our story match minus? Did we take away or add?'

mis.m: Writes a story with the numbers in it but no question, such as 'Sam has 6 dogs and 3 cats.'
mis.why: The student does not know a problem needs something to find out.
mis.fix: Ask 'What do we want to know?' and add a question frame at the end: 'How many ___?'

mis.m: Solves 15 - 8 by counting back and lands on 8.
mis.why: The student counts the starting number as the first step back.
mis.fix: Use a number line and have students jump, counting the jumps, not the numbers they land on.

cra.c: Students act out a number sentence with objects or classmates, then tell a story that matches what they did.
cra.r: Students draw a picture for their story and show the action, such as crossing out for take away.
cra.a: Students write or tell the story, write the number sentence and solve it, then check that the answer makes sense in the story.
cra.look: Students tell or write short stories that match a given number sentence and solve them with drawings or objects.

assess: How does your story match the minus sign?
What is the question in your story?
advance: Can you write a comparing story for the same number sentence?
Change the story so the answer is the missing start.

assess: Where in your picture is the 4 taken away?
What does the answer mean in your story?
advance: Can you tell a different story with the same numbers?
How did you solve it?

assess: What is happening in this number sentence?
Show me 9 cubes. Now take away 4.
advance: How many are left?
Tell me a story with 9 and 4.
support: Give a story frame: 'There were ___. Then ___. How many ___?'
Let students act out the story with toys before drawing it.

d: Generate and solve problem situations when given a number sentence involving addition or subtraction of numbers within 20.

mis.m: Says a nickel is worth more than a dime because it is bigger.
mis.why: The student links size to value, which works for many objects but not for coins.
mis.fix: Put a nickel and a dime next to 5 pennies and 10 pennies, and ask 'Which coin is worth the same as more pennies?'

mis.m: Mixes up a nickel and a quarter, or a penny and a nickel, by color or size.
mis.why: The coins look similar and students have not yet noticed the details.
mis.fix: Use a coin-sort mat with the front and back of each coin and have students describe the pictures and edges.

mis.m: Thinks every coin is worth 1 because each one is 'one coin.'
mis.why: The student counts coins instead of values.
mis.fix: Trade coins for pennies: one dime for 10 pennies, so the dime is worth 10 cents.

cra.c: Students sort real or play pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters, look closely at each side and trade coins for equal sets of pennies.
cra.r: Students match coin pictures to their values and draw how many pennies equal one coin.
cra.a: Students state relationships, such as '1 dime is worth the same as 2 nickels' and '5 pennies are worth 1 nickel.'
cra.look: Students name each coin by value, use magnifying glasses to describe coins and trade coins to show relationships.

assess: How many nickels make a dime? How do you know?
Why is a dime worth more than a nickel even though it is smaller?
advance: How many dimes would you trade for a quarter? Can you?
What coins could you use to make 25 cents?

assess: What is on the back of this coin?
How many pennies equal this coin?
advance: Which coin is worth the same as 5 pennies?
Can you show a dime a different way?

assess: Which coin is a penny? Point to it.
How much is a nickel worth?
advance: Is a nickel worth more or less than a dime?
Show me 5 pennies. Which coin is the same?
support: Introduce two coins at a time with a picture card for each.
Use large picture cards of coins with the value written below.

stems: This is a ___. It is worth ___ cents.
A ___ is worth more than a ___.
I know it is a ___ because ___.
d: Identify U.S. coins, including pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters, by value and describe the relationships among them.

mis.m: Writes the cent symbol before the number, such as ¢10.
mis.why: Students have seen the dollar sign before the number and copy that order.
mis.fix: Show price tags with the cent symbol after the number and say 'We say ten cents, so the cents come after.'

mis.m: Writes a dime as 1¢ because it is one coin.
mis.why: The student writes how many coins, not the value.
mis.fix: Ask 'How many cents is a dime worth?' and match it to 10 pennies before writing 10¢.

mis.m: Writes 5c, a dollar sign or just the number without the cent symbol.
mis.why: The cent symbol is new and easy to mix up with other marks.
mis.fix: Practice tracing the cent symbol on coin labels and post a model card with each coin and its value.

cra.c: Students set up a class store with real or play coins and price labels, and pick a coin to match each label.
cra.r: Students label pictures of coins with their value using the cent symbol.
cra.a: Students write the value of each coin, such as 1¢, 5¢, 10¢ and 25¢, and read it aloud.
cra.look: Students write values with the cent symbol after the number and read them as 'cents.'

assess: Why does the cent symbol go after the number?
How is 10¢ different from 1 dime?
advance: Write the value of a quarter. How do you know?
Which is worth more, 10¢ or 5¢? Show the coins.

assess: What coin is this? How do you write its value?
Read this label aloud.
advance: Can you make a label for a nickel?
What coin matches 25¢?

assess: Point to the cent symbol.
How much is a penny worth?
advance: Trace the cent symbol here.
Which coin is worth 10¢?
support: Give a coin card with the value written for students to copy.
Work with one coin at a time before mixing.

stems: I wrote the cent symbol after ___.
d: Write a number with the cent symbol to describe the value of a coin.

mis.m: Counts a dime, a nickel and a penny as 1, 2, 3 cents.
mis.why: The student counts coins, not their values.
mis.fix: Have students say the value of each coin before counting, then count on: 10, 15, 16.

mis.m: Mixes counting by tens and fives, such as dime, dime, nickel counted as 10, 20, 30.
mis.why: The student keeps the same skip count after the coin type changes.
mis.fix: Sort coins from greatest to least value first and change the count aloud when the coin changes: '10, 20 ... now nickels: 25.'

mis.m: Counts pennies first and then cannot switch to counting by tens for dimes.
mis.why: Starting with ones makes later skip counting harder.
mis.fix: Model lining up dimes, then nickels, then pennies, and count the largest value first.

cra.c: Students count real or play coin collections, sorting them by type and lining them up before counting.
cra.r: Students use a hundred chart or number line to show jumps of 10, 5 and 1 for each coin.
cra.a: Students write the total with the cent symbol and record counts, such as 10, 20, 25, 30, 31 = 31¢.
cra.look: Students sort coins, count the largest coin first, and switch skip counts when the coin changes.

assess: Why did you count the dimes first?
How did you know to switch to counting by fives?
advance: Can you make 35¢ in two different ways?
Which collection is worth more? How do you know?

assess: Show your jumps on the hundred chart.
What number did you land on after the dimes?
advance: What if you add one more nickel?
How many pennies would equal this total?

assess: Count these dimes with me: 10, 20 ...
What do we count by for nickels?
advance: Now count on the pennies.
How much is it all together?
support: Start with collections of just one coin type, then add a second type.
Give a counting strip with 10, 20, 30 to point to.

stems: The coins are worth ___¢ in all.
I switched to counting by ___ because ___.
d: Use relationships to count by twos, fives, and tens to determine the value of a collection of pennies, nickels, and/or dimes.

mis.m: When counting past 109, says '100, 200' or 'one hundred ten, one hundred twenty, ... ' skipping numbers.
mis.why: The pattern after 100 is new, and students repeat the decade pattern incorrectly.
mis.fix: Count on a 120 chart while pointing to each number and stopping to notice that 101 to 110 repeats the 1 to 10 pattern.

mis.m: When counting backward, skips the decade change, such as 52, 51, 50, 59, 58.
mis.why: Counting back across a ten is harder than counting forward.
mis.fix: Use a 120 chart and point up one row when counting back from 50, saying '50, 49' slowly.

mis.m: Can count from 1 but cannot start at a number like 87.
mis.why: The student relies on counting from the beginning of the sequence.
mis.fix: Practice 'start at' counts: hold up a card, say the number, and count on three numbers together.

cra.c: Students count real objects, jump on a floor number path or move a bead string forward and backward from any number.
cra.r: Students use a 120 chart to point while counting forward and backward and fill in missing numbers on number strips.
cra.a: Students say and write counting sequences from any starting number, such as 98, 99, 100, 101, and 64, 63, 62, 61.
cra.look: Students count aloud forward and backward from any number while pointing on a 120 chart or number path.

assess: What comes after 109? How do you know?
What pattern helps you count back from 70?
advance: What number comes 3 before 101?
How is counting from 100 to 110 like counting from 0 to 10?

assess: Where are you on the chart? Which way do you move to count back?
What number is just before 60?
advance: Can you fill in the missing numbers on this strip?
Start at 114 and count back 5.

assess: Start at 20. Count forward with me.
What comes next?
advance: Now count back from 20.
Point to the number we stopped on.
support: Use a number path with fewer numbers before the full chart.
Count together in a group before counting alone.

d: Recite numbers forward and backward from any given number between 1 and 120.

mis.m: Skip counts by fives but moves more than five objects for each count, ending with the wrong total.
mis.why: The student says the count without grouping the objects.
mis.fix: Have students make groups of five first, then touch each group while saying the count.

mis.m: Skip counts by twos to 20 and then goes back to counting by ones without noticing.
mis.why: The student does not yet have the skip-counting pattern past a familiar range.
mis.fix: Practice on a 120 chart by coloring every second number, then read the colored numbers aloud.

mis.m: For a collection with leftovers, counts the groups of ten but forgets the extra objects.
mis.why: The student stops when the skip count ends.
mis.fix: Ask 'Are there any objects not counted?' and have students count on by ones from the last skip count.

cra.c: Students group real objects such as beans, cubes or straws into twos, fives and tens and count the groups aloud.
cra.r: Students draw groups or color skip-count patterns on a 120 chart and use a number line with equal jumps.
cra.a: Students write the skip-count sequence and the total, such as 10, 20, 30, 35, 36, 37.
cra.look: Students make equal groups before counting and point to each group while skip counting.

assess: Why is counting by tens faster than counting by ones here?
How do you know you counted every object?
advance: Count the same collection by fives. Do you get the same total?
Which skip count would you use for 80 objects? Why?

assess: How many are in each group?
Show me your jumps on the number line.
advance: Can you count this a different way?
What pattern do you see on the chart?

assess: Count these pairs with me: 2, 4 ...
How many are in this group?
advance: Make one more group. What do we say next?
Are any left over?
support: Give a mat with circles for groups of 2, 5 or 10.
Practice the skip count aloud before counting objects.

stems: I had ___ left over, so I counted on.
d: Skip count by twos, fives, and tens to determine the total number of objects up to 120 in a set.

mis.m: Says 10 more than 46 is 47.
mis.why: The student confuses 10 more with 1 more.
mis.fix: Build 46 with base-ten blocks and add one ten-stick, then count the tens again.

mis.m: Counts on 10 by ones and gets lost, ending on 55 or 57.
mis.why: The student does not yet use place value and counts by ones.
mis.fix: Use a 120 chart to show that 10 more is the number just below, and point to how the tens digit changes.

mis.m: For 10 less than 105, says 905 or 15.
mis.why: Crossing the hundreds is new, and students are not sure which digit changes.
mis.fix: Build 105 as 10 tens and 5 ones, take away 1 ten and count what is left.

cra.c: Students build a number with base-ten blocks and add or take away one ten-stick, then name the new number.
cra.r: Students use a 120 chart to move down a row for 10 more and up a row for 10 less, or jump by 10 on a number line.
cra.a: Students write equations such as 46 + 10 = 56 and 46 - 10 = 36 and explain that the tens digit changes by 1.
cra.look: Students add or remove a ten and explain that only the tens digit changes.

assess: Why does only the tens digit change?
How can you find 10 less without counting?
advance: What is 20 more than 46? How do you know?
What number is 10 more than 110?

assess: Where did you move on the chart?
How many tens do you have now?
advance: What would happen if you added 10 again?
What is the pattern when you go up the chart?

assess: Show me 46 with blocks.
Add one ten. How many tens now?
advance: Is 56 more or less than 46?
Take one ten away. What number is it?
support: Use a 120 chart with the column highlighted.
Practice 1 more and 1 less before 10 more and 10 less.

stems: The tens digit changed from ___ to ___.
d: Use relationships to determine the number that is 10 more and 10 less than a given number up to 120.

mis.m: Writes 9 + 4 = 13 for 'Lily had 9 crayons. She gave 4 to Ana. How many does she have now?'
mis.why: The student sees two numbers and adds without thinking about the action.
mis.fix: Act it out with real crayons or counters and ask 'Did she get more or give some away?'

mis.m: Draws a picture with too many details, like faces on every person, and never gets to the math.
mis.why: The student thinks the picture needs to look real.
mis.fix: Model quick math drawings with circles or dots and say 'Math pictures are fast and show the numbers.'

mis.m: Writes the number sentence with the answer first, such as 13 = 9 + 4, and then says it is wrong.
mis.why: The student thinks equations can only be written one way.
mis.fix: Show that both ways are true with a balance or cubes, and accept answers on either side.

cra.c: Students act out the word problem with counters, cubes or real objects on a part-part-whole mat.
cra.r: Students draw quick pictures with circles, a number bond or a part-part-whole mat to show the problem.
cra.a: Students write the number sentence that matches their model, such as 12 - 5 = 7, and connect each number to the story.
cra.look: Students act out or draw the story and then write a number sentence, pointing to where each number comes from.

assess: How does your number sentence match your picture?
Why did you choose to subtract?
advance: Can you write another number sentence for the same story?
What would change if she got 4 more instead?

assess: What does each circle in your picture stand for?
Where is the answer in your drawing?
advance: Can you show the same problem a different way?
Which part of the story is the whole?

assess: How many crayons did she have first? Show me.
What happened next?
advance: Take away 4. How many are left?
Can you say it as a number sentence?
support: Read the story one sentence at a time while acting it out.
Give a part-part-whole mat with labels for each part.

d: Represent word problems involving addition and subtraction of whole numbers up to 20 using concrete and pictorial models and number sentences.

mis.m: Thinks the equal sign means 'the answer comes next,' so says 7 = 3 + 4 is wrong.
mis.why: Most equations students have seen show the answer after the equal sign.
mis.fix: Use a pan balance with cubes: put 7 on one side and 3 and 4 on the other, and show it balances.

mis.m: Fills in 3 + 4 = [ ] + 2 with 7.
mis.why: The student adds the numbers on the left and stops at the equal sign.
mis.fix: Ask 'Is 3 + 4 the same as 7 + 2?' and build both sides with cubes to check.

mis.m: Says 5 + 2 = 2 + 5 is not true because the numbers are in a different order.
mis.why: The student looks at how the sides look instead of their values.
mis.fix: Build both sides with cubes and count each side to see that they are the same amount.

cra.c: Students use a pan balance or a cube balance to show that each side has the same amount, such as 6 + 2 and 4 + 4.
cra.r: Students draw two groups of dots or cubes for each side of the equation and check that they match.
cra.a: Students decide if equations are true or false, such as 8 = 5 + 3 and 4 + 3 = 6 + 1, and explain using 'the same as.'
cra.look: Students check both sides of an equation with a balance or drawings and read the equal sign as 'is the same as.'

assess: How do you know both sides are the same?
Why is 8 = 5 + 3 true?
advance: Make your own true equation with two numbers on each side.
What could go in the box: 6 + 2 = [ ] + 5?

assess: How does your drawing show each side?
How many are on this side? On that side?
advance: Is 4 + 4 = 5 + 2 true or false? Show me.
Can you change one number to make it true?

assess: Show me 5 on this side and 5 on that side. Does it balance?
What does the equal sign mean?
advance: Are these the same amount?
Is this side more or less?
support: Use a real pan balance before drawings.
Read the equal sign aloud as 'is the same as' every time.

stems: The equal sign means is the same as.
d: Understand that the equal sign represents a relationship where expressions on each side of the equal sign represent the same value(s).

mis.m: For [ ] - 4 = 9, writes 5 in the box.
mis.why: The student subtracts the two numbers shown instead of thinking about what the whole must be.
mis.fix: Use a part-part-whole mat and ask 'What number did we start with if we took away 4 and had 9 left?'

mis.m: For 5 + [ ] + 2 = 10, writes 17 or 7.
mis.why: The student adds all the numbers shown or ignores one of the terms.
mis.fix: Build the 5 and 2 with cubes, then add cubes until there are 10, counting how many were added.

mis.m: For 12 = [ ] + 8, says the equation is backward and cannot be solved.
mis.why: The student expects the answer to be on the right side.
mis.fix: Read it aloud as '12 is the same as what and 8?' and model it with a balance or ten frames.

cra.c: Students use cubes, counters or a pan balance to find the missing number, adding or taking away until both sides match.
cra.r: Students draw a part-part-whole mat, a number bond or a number line and mark the missing part with a box.
cra.a: Students write the missing number and check it by reading the full equation aloud, such as 13 - [5] = 8.
cra.look: Students model the equation, find the missing part and check by putting the number back in the equation.

assess: How did you check your answer?
Is the missing part a part or the whole? How do you know?
advance: Can you write a story that matches this equation?
What if the box was in a different place? Show me.

assess: Where is the missing part in your number bond?
What number did you start with?
advance: Can you solve it a different way?
How does adding help you solve this subtraction?

assess: Show me 9 cubes. How many more to make 13?
What does the box mean?
advance: Put your number in the box. Is it true?
Count with me.
support: Start with the box at the end, then move it to the middle and the start.
Give a number bond template to fill in.

d: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation when the unknown may be any one of the three or four terms in the equation.
